summary: For ages 6–7 (UK Year 2): count in 3s forwards and backwards from 0, extending equal-groups thinking to a less familiar step size and seeding the 3× table and the idea of 'a third'. The central insight is that multiples of 3 still form a regular pattern — a diagonal pattern of repeating parallel lines on a hundred square — even though they do not line up in neat columns like 2s, 5s and 10s. Each step should be tied to one more group of three, and backward counting and mid-sequence continuation practised as skills in their own right.
misconceptions: Feeling 3s have 'no pattern' because they don't form neat columns (they form diagonals).
Reciting 3s as isolated rote with no link to groups of three or the 3× table.
Being able to count forward but not backward in 3s.
Losing the step when crossing a decade (…18, 21…) — miscounting the +3 across the ten.

activities.title: The diagonal reveal: shading 3s on a hundred square
steps: Step forward in 3s from 0 (3, 6, 9, 12…), shading or marking each multiple on a hundred square as you say it.
Notice that, unlike the vertical columns 5s and 10s make, the multiples of 3 march down the grid as repeating parallel diagonal lines (a diagonal pattern).
Use the diagonal pattern to predict the next multiple before you reach it, then check.
Play 'spot the multiple of 3' by pointing to multiples anywhere on the grid, not only counting up from 0.
Pay special attention to crossing each decade (…18, 21… and …27, 30…) so the +3 step is not lost across the ten.
activities.insight: Multiples of 3 are patterned, not random — the diagonal pattern lets you predict the next multiple and recognise multiples anywhere, countering the feeling that '3s have no pattern'.

activities.title: Number-line 3-jumps and groups of three
steps: Make equal jumps of 3 along a number line, saying the multiple you land on each time.
For each jump, add one more group of three — show it with an array or counters (three counters per group) alongside the jump.
Connect 'four jumps of 3' to 'four groups of three' (four threes make 12) and to building up the 3× table.
Briefly link three equal groups making a whole to the idea of 'a third'.
activities.insight: Each step of 3 is one more group of three; stepping in 3s is the foundation of the 3× table and connects to thirds.

activities.title: Counting back and entering mid-sequence
steps: Count backwards in 3s from a multiple: 30, 27, 24… down to 0, using physical or drawn hops back along a number line.
Practise short backward runs (e.g. 12 → 0) as their own skill, not expecting it to come free with forward counting.
Continue a sequence from the middle: given 12, 15, 18, say the next number (and keep going) without restarting from 3.
Say the number just before a given multiple (e.g. what comes before 12 in the 3s).
activities.insight: Backward counting and continuing from any point are separate skills: the step is always +3 (or −3), so you can add or subtract 3 from the last number rather than restarting.

activities.title: Retrieval and oral fluency
steps: Answer quick questions: 'What is the next number in 3s?', fill a missing multiple in a sequence, put multiples of 3 in order, and count back in 3s.
With a partner, count aloud in 3s forwards and backwards, taking turns to say the next number.
Answer 'What's 3 more than 18?' (21) and 'What comes just before 12 in the 3s?' (9).
activities.insight: Fluency means stepping by three both ways and entering the sequence at any point, not only chanting up from 0.

checkQuestion: Count in 3s from 0 up to 30. Now count backwards in 3s from 30 down to 0. Then here's part of a sequence — 12, 15, 18, __ — tell me the next number and keep it going. (Watch for sub-counting by ones, whether backward holds, and whether they can continue from mid-sequence.)
checkAnswer: Recites 3, 6, 9, …, 30 and back 30, 27, …, 0 without sub-counting each interval by ones; continues 12, 15, 18, 21… — stepping by three each time.
